quests.hint: The feeling that makes your stomach growl and sends you looking for a snack.
quests.explanation: Hungry pairs with 'starving' for extra emphasis — 'I'm absolutely starving' is a common, more dramatic way to say the same thing.
quests.textToSpeak: After skipping lunch, I was very ___ by the time dinner was ready.
quests.correctAnswer: After skipping lunch, I was very hungry by the time dinner was ready.

quests.hint: The feeling that makes you reach for a glass of water without thinking twice.
quests.explanation: Thirsty describes wanting a drink. 'Parched' is an informal, more intense version — 'I'm absolutely parched' after a hot walk.
quests.textToSpeak: After the long run in the heat, I was extremely ___ and drank two glasses of water.
quests.correctAnswer: After the long run in the heat, I was extremely thirsty and drank two glasses of water.

quests.hint: Heavy eyelids and a yawn you can't hold back.
quests.explanation: Sleepy is milder than 'exhausted' — it simply means you're ready for bed, not necessarily worn out from effort.
quests.textToSpeak: I felt very ___ after staying up late watching films the night before.
quests.correctAnswer: I felt very sleepy after staying up late watching films the night before.

quests.hint: A large public vehicle that stops along a set route to pick up passengers.
quests.explanation: We say 'catch the bus' or 'take the bus,' and 'by bus' describes the method of travel — 'I go to work by bus.'
quests.textToSpeak: I catch the number fourteen ___ every morning to get to the office on time.
quests.correctAnswer: I catch the number fourteen bus every morning to get to the office on time.

quests.hint: Runs on tracks and is often the quickest way to travel between city centres.
quests.explanation: 'By train' is the standard way to describe this journey. 'Catch a train' and 'miss a train' are two phrases you'll use constantly.
quests.textToSpeak: The fastest way to get to the city centre from here is by ___.
quests.correctAnswer: The fastest way to get to the city centre from here is by train.

quests.hint: A car you can hire on the spot to take you exactly where you need to go.
quests.explanation: 'Take a taxi' or 'call a taxi' are the ones you'll hear most. Americans often say 'cab' instead.
quests.textToSpeak: We decided to take a ___ because we had far too much luggage to carry.
quests.correctAnswer: We decided to take a taxi because we had far too much luggage to carry.

quests.hint: The word that turns a demand into a polite request.
quests.explanation: Please softens a request and usually goes at the end of a sentence in casual speech, as in 'Pass the salt, please.'
quests.textToSpeak: Could you pass me the salt, ___? I appreciate your help very much.
quests.correctAnswer: Could you pass me the salt, please? I appreciate your help very much.

quests.hint: What you say the moment you realise you've made someone wait.
quests.explanation: 'I'm sorry' apologises for something you did; 'I'm sorry to hear that' expresses sympathy for someone else's bad news — two very different uses.
quests.textToSpeak: I am so ___ that I am late - the traffic on the way here was terrible.
quests.correctAnswer: I am so sorry that I am late - the traffic on the way here was terrible.

quests.hint: The reply you give right after someone thanks you.
quests.explanation: 'You're welcome' is the standard response to 'thank you.' 'No problem' and 'not at all' are more casual alternatives.
quests.textToSpeak: You are very ___ - it was truly my pleasure to help you today.
quests.correctAnswer: You are very welcome - it was truly my pleasure to help you today.

quests.hint: Getting somewhere well before the expected time.
quests.explanation: Early works as both adjective and adverb without changing form — 'an early train' and 'arrive early' use the exact same word.
quests.textToSpeak: She always arrives ___ to make sure she gets a good seat at the front.
quests.correctAnswer: She always arrives early to make sure she gets a good seat at the front.

quests.hint: Behind schedule, with the clock working against you.
quests.explanation: 'Running late' is the phrase you'll hear constantly — it means you're behind schedule and hurrying to catch up.
quests.textToSpeak: He was running ___ and had to sprint to catch the last train of the evening.
quests.correctAnswer: He was running late and had to sprint to catch the last train of the evening.

quests.hint: Getting something done with real speed and no wasted time.
quests.explanation: Quickly is the adverb form of 'quick.' It describes how an action is done, not the thing itself — 'she worked quickly,' not 'she is quickly.'
quests.textToSpeak: She finished the whole assignment very ___ and still had time to check it.
quests.correctAnswer: She finished the whole assignment very quickly and still had time to check it.

quests.hint: An open green space in a town where people walk, sit, and play.
quests.explanation: 'In the park' and 'go to the park' are the standard patterns. British parks are often free, public spaces open to everyone.
quests.textToSpeak: On weekends, I enjoy taking my dog for a walk in the ___ near our house.
quests.correctAnswer: On weekends, I enjoy taking my dog for a walk in the park near our house.

quests.hint: A place with stalls selling fresh food, often only open on certain days.
quests.explanation: Market can mean a physical place to shop or the wider idea of buying and selling — 'the housing market' uses the second sense.
quests.textToSpeak: The local ___ sells fresh fruit, vegetables, and flowers every Saturday morning.
quests.correctAnswer: The local market sells fresh fruit, vegetables, and flowers every Saturday morning.

quests.hint: The shop you visit to collect medicine a doctor has prescribed.
quests.explanation: Pharmacy is the standard term; 'chemist's' is the more traditional British word for the same place.
quests.textToSpeak: I need to collect my prescription from the ___ on the way home from work.
quests.correctAnswer: I need to collect my prescription from the pharmacy on the way home from work.

quests.hint: The part of the day between waking up and lunchtime.
quests.explanation: 'In the morning' is the standard phrase, but we switch to 'on' before a named day — 'on Monday morning.'
quests.textToSpeak: I prefer to exercise in the ___ when I feel most alert and energetic.
quests.correctAnswer: I prefer to exercise in the morning when I feel most alert and energetic.

quests.hint: The stretch of the day after lunch and before evening sets in.
quests.explanation: 'In the afternoon' follows the same rule as morning, switching to 'on' before a named day — 'on Tuesday afternoon.'
quests.textToSpeak: She has her piano lessons every Tuesday ___ after school finishes at three.
quests.correctAnswer: She has her piano lessons every Tuesday afternoon after school finishes at three.

quests.hint: When the sun goes down and the day starts winding to a close.
quests.explanation: 'In the evening' is standard, but 'Good evening' is a fixed greeting used on its own, without 'in.'
quests.textToSpeak: In the ___, we usually relax and watch something on television together.
quests.correctAnswer: In the evening, we usually relax and watch something on television together.

quests.hint: The colour of ripe tomatoes, stop signs, and roses.
quests.explanation: Red can also describe embarrassment — 'she went red' means she blushed, not that her skin changed permanently!
quests.textToSpeak: She wore a stunning ___ dress to the dinner party on Saturday evening.
quests.correctAnswer: She wore a stunning red dress to the dinner party on Saturday evening.

quests.hint: The colour of a clear daytime sky.
quests.explanation: Blue also describes sadness in English — 'feeling blue' is a common idiom for feeling a little down.
quests.textToSpeak: The ___ sky was completely clear without a single cloud visible all day.
quests.correctAnswer: The blue sky was completely clear without a single cloud visible all day.

quests.hint: The colour of fresh grass and leaves.
quests.explanation: Green also means environmentally friendly — 'going green' — and a 'green light' means permission to proceed.
quests.textToSpeak: The hills were covered in lush ___ grass after all the recent heavy rain.
quests.correctAnswer: The hills were covered in lush green grass after all the recent heavy rain.

quests.hint: A round fruit, often red or green, that grows on trees.
quests.explanation: 'An apple' takes 'an' because it starts with a vowel sound. The famous saying is 'an apple a day keeps the doctor away.'
quests.textToSpeak: An ___ a day keeps the doctor away - or so the old saying tells us.
quests.correctAnswer: An apple a day keeps the doctor away - or so the old saying tells us.

quests.hint: The natural stimulant found in coffee, tea, and many soft drinks.
quests.explanation: 'Caffeine-free' describes drinks without it, and 'sensitive to caffeine' describes someone easily affected by it.
quests.textToSpeak: She stopped consuming ___ after realising it was seriously affecting her sleep.
quests.correctAnswer: She stopped consuming caffeine after realising it was seriously affecting her sleep.

quests.hint: The sweet ingredient many people are told to eat less of.
quests.explanation: 'Cut down on sugar' and 'sugar-free' are two of the most common health-related phrases involving this word.
quests.textToSpeak: The doctor strongly advised him to cut down on ___ for health reasons.
quests.correctAnswer: The doctor strongly advised him to cut down on sugar for health reasons.

quests.hint: Someone you choose to spend time with and trust.
quests.explanation: 'Close friend' and 'best friend' show different levels of closeness. 'Make friends' is the phrase for building new relationships.
quests.textToSpeak: She is my closest ___ - we have known each other since primary school.
quests.correctAnswer: She is my closest friend - we have known each other since primary school.

quests.hint: The person who lives right next door to you.
quests.explanation: Neighbour is spelled with a 'u' in British English ('neighbor' in American English) — the pronunciation stays exactly the same.
quests.textToSpeak: Our ___ always waters our plants when we go away on holiday.
quests.correctAnswer: Our neighbour always waters our plants when we go away on holiday.

quests.hint: Someone you work alongside, though not necessarily a close friend.
quests.explanation: Colleague is more formal and workplace-specific than 'coworker,' which is more common in American English.
quests.textToSpeak: My ___ helped me finish the urgent report when I was running out of time.
quests.correctAnswer: My colleague helped me finish the urgent report when I was running out of time.

quests.hint: A price so low it feels like a bargain.
quests.explanation: Cheap can sound negative about quality, so 'affordable' or 'good value' are gentler alternatives when you mean well-priced rather than poor.
quests.textToSpeak: She found a very ___ flight online and booked it immediately before it sold out.
quests.correctAnswer: She found a very cheap flight online and booked it immediately before it sold out.

quests.hint: Free of dirt, mess, and anything out of place.
quests.explanation: 'Keep clean' and 'clean up' are the phrases you'll use most — the second one describes the actual act of tidying.
quests.textToSpeak: Please keep the shared kitchen ___ so that everyone can use it comfortably.
quests.correctAnswer: Please keep the shared kitchen clean so that everyone can use it comfortably.

quests.hint: So little noise you could hear a pin drop.
quests.explanation: 'Keep quiet' means stop talking, while simply 'be quiet' is a direct, sometimes blunt, request for silence.
quests.textToSpeak: The library must be kept ___ so that everyone can concentrate properly.
quests.correctAnswer: The library must be kept quiet so that everyone can concentrate properly.
